stories.title: KDDI names Kohtaro Murasawa CEO of KDDI America and Telehouse America
stories.summary: Global executive to accelerate drive of IoT, cybersecurity, peering and global messaging growth in the Americas NEW YORK, NY— read more...
stories.content:
October 1, 2026
#### **Global executive to accelerate drive of IoT, cybersecurity, peering and global messaging growth in the Americas**

**NEW YORK, NY—** KDDI Corporation announced the appointment of Kohtaro Murasawa as President and Chief Executive Officer of KDDI America, Inc. and Telehouse America, effective immediately, reinforcing its commitment to expanding advanced ICT and digital infrastructure services across the Americas. Murasawa succeeds Satoshi Oishi, who will return to Japan to take on a new leadership role within KDDI.

Murasawa brings more than three decades of international leadership experience within KDDI, with roles spanning the United States, Europe and Japan. He has previously led global enterprise initiatives, scaled multinational customer engagement and delivered network, IoT and data center solutions for organizations operating in varied and complex environments.

Most recently, Murasawa served as Deputy General Manager of KDDI’s Public Sector and Financial Industry Business Division, where he oversaw sales operations for corporate, government and major financial institution clients. In this role, he led delivery of advanced WAN, IoT and data center solutions to highly regulated industries.

“KDDI America and Telehouse America are ideal partners to our customers’ global growth strategies,” said Kohtaro Murasawa. “We will scale our capabilities in digital transformation, cybersecurity, IoT and digital infrastructure while strengthening our colocation and interconnection platforms to meet rising demand for secure, high-performance global services.”

Murasawa added, “Our priority is to deliver integrated, end-to-end solutions that simplify complexity for enterprises operating across borders. By combining connectivity, advanced technologies and global operational expertise, we will drive measurable outcomes for our customers and expand our leadership in the digital infrastructure market.”

Satoshi Oishi leaves the role following a successful tenure in which he sharpened the organizations’ strategic direction and expanded their presence in key growth areas.

“It has been a privilege to lead these organizations,” said Satoshi Oishi. “Together, we have enhanced our service capabilities, strengthened partnerships, and reinforced our foundation for continued success. I am confident that KDDI America and Telehouse America will continue to deliver exceptional value to our customers under Murasawa’s leadership.”

KDDI America and Telehouse America are committed to advancing customer success in a rapidly changing digital landscape. Through a customer-first approach, the organizations deliver integrated solutions across network, cloud, IoT, AI, cybersecurity, global messaging along with colocation and interconnection services—enabling enterprises to operate with greater speed, security and scale. Backed by Telehouse America’s carrier-neutral data centers and robust peering ecosystem, KDDI America continues to power seamless global connectivity and drive meaningful business outcomes.

### About KDDI America

KDDI America is a global leader in information and communication technology (ICT) solutions. As a subsidiary of KDDI Corporation, one of Japan’s largest telecommunications companies and a Fortune Global 500 Company, KDDI America delivers a broad range of services, including cloud solutions, networking, cybersecurity, and managed IT services. With a focus on connecting businesses worldwide and enabling digital transformation, KDDI America empowers organizations to enhance their capabilities, scale their operations, and innovate for the future.

Learn more at us.kddi.com

### About Telehouse America

Telehouse is a leading global data center service provider under KDDI Group, bringing together more than 3,000 business partners including carriers, mobile and content providers, enterprises, cloud providers and financial services companies. Established in 1989, Telehouse provides reliable, secure, and flexible colocation services, enabling organizations to accelerate speed to market and create business opportunities through fast, efficient and secure interconnections.

For more information, please visit: www.telehouse.com

### About KDDI Corporation

KDDI is a leading Japanese telecommunications company with over 100 million customers. In recent years, KDDI has expanded beyond its core telecommunications business into areas such as AI, finance, energy, retail, and cybersecurity, contributing to structural reforms across various industries. Globally, KDDI provides mobile services, IoT services for connected cars, and data center connectivity, primarily in North America, Europe, and Asia. KDDI is driving social impact and transformation through its mid-term management strategy, “Power-to-Connect 2028.” For more information, visit the KDDI website: https://www.kddi.com/english

stories.title: Tencent signs on for 100,000 GPUs via Oracle
stories.summary: Tencent has reportedly committed to a deal to access 100,000 Nvidia GPUs through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, one of the largest single GPU procurement arrangements by a Chinese technology company since US export controls tightened. The arrangement allows Tencent to secure cutting-edge AI compute via a US-based cloud provider rather than purchasing hardware directly, circumventing restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.
stories.why_it_matters: This deal formalizes a loophole in the US export control regime: Chinese AI ambitions increasingly run through rented American cloud capacity rather than shipped hardware. It hands Oracle a marquee customer and billions in revenue, puts pressure on Washington to close or regulate 'compute-as-a-service' workarounds, and accelerates the GPU scarcity race among Western cloud providers competing for the same silicon.
stories.content:
Tencent has reportedly signed a contract to access 100,000 GPUs via Oracle's cloud platform.

As reported by the Financial Times, and citing two people familiar with the matter, Tencent has signed a five-year lease across multiple Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia.

The lease will enable Tencent to access Oracle's GPUs in the data centers, which are not available in China due to the US' export controls on the hardware, and is hoped to help Tencent to advance its AI models and agentic tools.

The sources told the FT that the deal was valued at around $7bn, with Tencent paying 30 percent upfront.

*DCD* has contacted Oracle and Tencent for comment.

The Chinese cloud, social media and gaming company reported a negative cash flow of RMB 13.8 billion ($2.06bn) for its second quarter, which, according to the FT, is the company's first negative figure in more than a decade. Speaking on that, CFO John Lo said at the time of the earnings call that this was "reflecting large AI infrastructure capex and AI-related prepayments," and that "excluding the prepayments for compute procurement, free cash flow would have been RMB 37.6bn ($5.61bn)," making the difference in the realm of $7-8bn.

Tencent president Martin Lau said: "We're comfortable in making significant investments in AI because not only is there a substantial upside potential, there is also clear downside protection. The AI investments we're making are mostly in AI infrastructure, and in the worst case, which we do not believe would happen, we can choose to rent that infrastructure out at cost recovery or even better prices via Tencent Cloud if needed."

While that is a possibility, executives made it clear that the current intention for that compute is for "training bigger and better Hunyuan models," followed by inferencing workloads and later to rent out as bare metal or via Model-as-a-Service offerings.

This is consistent with the company's previously stated strategy, with Tencent saying that it had focused on developing its internal services. In May 2026, Tencent CSO James Mitchell said: "Looking through the rest of this year, as the supply of China-designed GPUs progressively ramps up, we'll be remedying that situation; we will be making more capacity available in Tencent Cloud, and consequently driving up Tencent Cloud's rate of expansion. That's where the trade-off has been made: we have been consciously late to monetize the AI opportunity through Tencent Cloud because we've been simultaneously supporting a number of AI initiatives internally."

stories.summary_zh: 据报道，Tencent 已达成一项协议，将通过 Oracle Cloud Infrastructure 获得 10 万块 Nvidia GPU 的访问权，这是自美国出口管制收紧以来中国科技公司规模最大的单笔 GPU 采购安排之一。该安排使 Tencent 能够通过一家美国云服务提供商获得尖端 AI 算力，而非直接购买硬件，从而绕过了对向中国出售先进芯片的限制。
stories.why_zh: 这笔交易将美国出口管制体系中的一个漏洞正式化:中国的AI雄心正越来越多地通过租用美国cloud算力而非购买硬件来实现。它为Oracle带来了一个标杆客户和数十亿美元的收入,给华盛顿施加了封堵或监管'compute-as-a-service'(算力即服务)绕道模式的压力,并加速了西方cloud服务商之间争夺同一批芯片的GPU稀缺竞赛。

stories.title: Firmus on track for $43.7b valuation, dividing the ASX's big investors
stories.summary: Australian AI data centre and infrastructure company Firmus is reportedly on track to reach a A$43.7 billion valuation, a figure that has split the country's largest institutional investors ahead of its expected ASX listing. The lofty number reflects surging appetite for AI-related assets but has also drawn skepticism from some funds concerned about whether such multiples can be sustained.
stories.why_it_matters: Firmus' valuation divide is a test case for whether the AI infrastructure boom translates into durable public-market value or echoes past tech froth. A successful listing at this scale would validate Australia's data centre build-out and pull more capital into APAC AI infrastructure, while a stumble could chill IPO appetite across the region's whole sector.
stories.content:
Firmus Technologies could become the second-biggest float in Australian sharemarket history after targeting a market capitalisation of $43.7 billion when it debuts next month amid intense debate among the country’s major investors over whether the neocloud hopeful is a buy or bust.

The company, which operates data centres in Singapore and Melbourne and rents out its specialised processing chips to large technology companies like Meta Platforms, priced its initial public offering at $11 per share, as first reported by *The Australian Financial Review* on Thursday.

stories.title: A data centre in Kurri Kurri: your questions answered
stories.summary: AirTrunk chief customer officer Rob Bartrop addressed community questions about the company's proposed data centre in Kurri Kurri, in the NSW Hunter region, in a piece originally published in the Newcastle Herald. The facility is framed as part of the digital backbone supporting everyday services — from banking and healthcare appointments to streaming and AI — and the article responds directly to local concerns about what the project means for the community.
stories.why_it_matters: Regional Australian data centre projects increasingly live or die on social license, not just planning approvals. AirTrunk's public-facing Q&A signals an industry shift toward proactive community engagement as Hunter Valley locals weigh jobs and investment against power, water, and land-use concerns — a template other operators facing regional opposition will be watching closely.
stories.content:
This article first appeared in Newcastle Herald on 23 September – read here.

*AirTrunk’s Rob Bartrop explains the proposed Kurri Kurri data centre and what it could mean for the local community.*

Whether we are paying a bill, making an appointment, watching a movie with the kids, accessing government services or using artificial intelligence, most of us rely on digital services multiple times every day.

The computers behind those services once sat under our desks or in server rooms in our office buildings. As more of our lives and work move online, more information needs to be stored and processed.

That is why more data centres are being built.

They are purpose-built facilities filled with computers that ensure the apps and services we use are available, secure and responsive when we need them.

Running them together in this way can be more than seven times as energy efficient as running them in our homes or workplaces.

Our business – AirTrunk – started in Sydney and builds and operates data centres across the Asia-Pacific region, and we’re proposing to build one in Kurri Kurri.

Kurri Kurri has an established industrial base and the infrastructure needed to support the proposal.

But those factors do not answer the local questions, and what it means for Kurri Kurri.

If a large development were proposed near my home, I’d want to know how it would affect local jobs, businesses, energy, water and the area’s future.

Over the past few months, we have spoken with residents, local organisations and businesses to understand what’s top of mind.

I want to share some of what we’ve heard and how it is shaping the proposal.

The proposal is for a two-storey data centre on part of the former Kurri Kurri smelter site. It would connect directly to existing high-voltage power infrastructure adjacent to the site, and use land previously occupied by the smelter.

We have had a lot of questions about noise and proximity to nearby residents. This is actually a big reason why we selected the old smelter site -the nearest homes are more than 500 metres away, and the site is located right in the heart of an industrial zone in-between a power station and the four-lane Hunter Expressway.

But we know distance alone does not answer every concern. Noise from the facility, including equipment and generator testing, will be assessed as part of the planning process, with measures included in the design to keep it within the required limits.

We’ll also put a lot of thought and effort into the outside design and landscaping to ensure it’s a facility that our employees are proud to come to work at.

If approved, the facility will provide more than 350 ongoing jobs for decades to come, as well as several thousand jobs during construction. We know this because we are a long-term operator of data centres, and know that we need a lot of ongoing support – ranging from trades to maintenance, security and a range of support services.

And we are keen to make those jobs available to the local community and are working with trade colleges, TAFE, local businesses and our procurement teams to make sure we invest in pathways and job placements to provide every opportunity for local participation.

People have also asked whether the project will add to their power bills. It won’t. AirTrunk will pay our own way for all of the costs to connect to the grid.

We are speaking with renewable energy developers about unlocking new projects in the Hunter Renewable Energy Zone and other parts of the state.

Beyond that, we’ve committed to launching a Community Energy Program that would fund a community battery for local Kurri residents, resulting in a $200 annual deduction from each participating household’s electricity bill.

Water is another question we hear regularly. The proposed facility would use air cooling and consume minimal water during operations.

If AirTrunk is going to operate in Kurri Kurri for decades, we should make a lasting commitment to public facilities that will benefit local residents.

That is why we have been working with Cessnock City Council on a proposed contribution of more than $37 million for district infrastructure, including more than $12 million to support the proposed Loxford District Sporting and Multipurpose Community Facility.

Our overall proposal still has to go through the planning process, and people will continue to have the opportunity to ask questions and raise concerns.

My focus is on what this project could mean for people who live and work here over the next 20 or 30 years, and how local people can take part in the opportunities it creates.

We’ll keep speaking with residents, businesses and local organisations about jobs, training, community facilities, energy and water.

In October, the AirTrunk team and I will be at the Kurri Kurri Visitor Information Centre. Come by if you have a question or want to share your view.

There is more to work through, and we’ll keep people informed as the proposal develops.
stories.title_zh: Kurri Kurri数据中心项目：常见问题解答
stories.summary_zh: AirTrunk 首席客户官 Rob Bartrop 在一篇最初发表于《Newcastle Herald》的文章中，回应了社区对该公司拟建于新南威尔士州 Hunter 地区 Kurri Kurri 的数据中心的提问。该设施被定位为支撑日常服务的数字骨干的一部分——从银行业务、医疗预约到流媒体和 AI——文章直接回应了当地民众对该项目对社区意味着什么的关切。
stories.why_zh: 澳大利亚区域data centre项目的成败越来越取决于社会认可度,而不仅仅是规划审批。AirTrunk面向公众的问答释放出行业转向主动社区沟通的信号——Hunter Valley当地居民正在权衡就业与投资机遇和电力、水资源及土地使用方面的担忧——这一做法将成为其他面临区域反对声音的运营商密切关注的范本。
